title: Influence of database accuracy on two-dimensional ray-tracing-based predictions in urban microcells
relevance_reason: The term 'vector database' in this paper refers to geometric building representations (building vectors, vertices, wall polygons) used for radio propagation modeling, not to vector databases for similarity search or nearest neighbor search. The paper has no connection to vector indexing, embedding-based search, or vector database technology.
research_focus: The influence of database accuracy (building layout geometry, electrical characteristics, base station locations) on the quality of two-dimensional ray-tracing-based radio propagation predictions in urban microcellular environments.
method: Ray-tracing prediction models (including reflection and diffraction) were run using building databases of varying accuracy (cadastre map, city map, 1:25000 scaled map) and with injected random errors in building geometry. Predictions were compared against field measurements to quantify sensitivity to database inaccuracies.
application_domain: Radio wave propagation modeling and urban microcell planning
results_summary: The paper quantified how inaccuracies in building geometry databases affect ray-tracing prediction accuracy in urban microcells. It found that predictions are more sensitive to errors in building corner (vertex) positions than to errors in building size, because corner errors change wall orientation. The most precise map (cadastre) yielded the best predictions, and the model was sensitive to the choice of reflection coefficient but not to small base station location variations. Error thresholds were established: 95% of building walls within 2 m or 95% of vertices within 1 m keeps the standard deviation increase below 1 dB. The study also confirmed that specular reflection per Fresnel law is an important propagation phenomenon in microcells.
limitations: The model does not consider trees or other neglected effects that may affect propagation; The study was conducted in a single specific environment (Bern), limiting generalizability; A scalar reflection coefficient independent of incidence angle decreases computation time but leads to less satisfactory predictions
research_gaps: Similar investigations in different environments are needed to determine how error thresholds depend on the environment; Effects of trees and other neglected phenomena need to be incorporated into the model

title: A reliable knowledge processing framework for combustion science using foundation models
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about a RAG framework and LLM application in combustion science; the vector database is used only as a retrieval component within the pipeline and is not analyzed, compared, or studied as a subject in its own right. No vector database systems, indexing methods, or similarity search algorithms are discussed in depth.
research_focus: Development of a RAG-based private knowledge processing framework for combustion science (specifically oblique detonation waves) using foundation models, with emphasis on mitigating hallucination and improving response accuracy through prompt engineering and external knowledge retrieval.
method: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline combining an open-source offline LLM (LlaMA-2 7B) with an embedding model (bge-base-en-v1.5 from BAAI), text segmentation with optimized chunk sizes and overlap, prompt engineering strategies, and a custom detection algorithm to filter out false research articles from generated responses.
mentioned_systems: LlaMA-2 7B; bge-base-en-v1.5; ChatGPT; GPT-3.5; GPT-4; Eliza; LoRA
application_domain: Combustion science, specifically oblique detonation waves (ODWs) and detonation-driven propulsion
results_summary: The paper develops and evaluates a RAG-based framework for processing combustion science literature, demonstrating that the framework-based model produces significantly more accurate and well-referenced responses compared to a standard LLM relying solely on internal knowledge. A custom detection algorithm was implemented to eliminate false or plagiarized research articles from generated responses, and the framework showed no indication of false articles when using this algorithm. However, repeated runs revealed instances where cited articles were inaccurately represented, and the cosine similarity metric used for retrieval was noted to potentially understate word frequency. The study also found that the framework exhibits hesitancy in generating novel arguments and that prompt format significantly influences response quality.
limitations: Cosine similarity metric used for retrieval may understate the frequency of words; The language model's temperature parameter could be further tuned for more innovative responses; The framework currently lacks any form of chat memory; The embedding model concentrates exclusively on textual embedding, excluding plots, tables, and mathematical equations; Repeated runs reveal instances where cited articles are inaccurately represented
research_gaps: Implementing a memory-based chat system to track evolution of knowledge processing and enable data lineage; Incorporating a multimodal embedding strategy encompassing plots, tables, and mathematical equations; Switching the base LLM to access more data and generate richer responses; Further tuning of the temperature parameter for more innovative domain-specific responses

title: Augmenting LLMs to Securely Retrieve Information for Construction and Facility Management
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about building and evaluating a RAG system for construction and facility management; Milvus is mentioned only as a storage/retrieval component in the pipeline without any in-depth analysis, comparison, or discussion of vector database technology.
research_focus: Design and evaluation of a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system for secure, domain-specific information retrieval in construction and facility management, integrating proprietary documents such as operation manuals, blueprints, and inspection results.
method: A RAG pipeline was built using the Mixtral 8x7B model for multilingual text processing and the Milvus vector database for document storage and retrieval. The system was evaluated using quantitative metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, semantic similarity) and qualitative human-like assessments on question-answer pairs generated for facility management tasks.
application_domain: Construction and facility management (operation manuals, inspection results, blueprints, technical drawings)
results_summary: The RAG system was implemented entirely with open-source components to ensure data security within a private perimeter. Evaluation showed strong performance in fluency (97% above 7/10) and relevance (83% above 7/10), but weaker results in factual accuracy (60% fully or almost accurate). The authors conclude that while the system enhances operational efficiency, notable challenges remain in lexical precision and factual accuracy. They recommend further refinement of retrieval and generation processes, including fine-tuning embedding models and chunk sizes, and integrating structured BIM data via function-calling.
limitations: Notable challenges in maintaining lexical precision and factual accuracy of generated answers; Restriction to PDF files, limiting handling of heterogeneous file types in construction projects; Need for further refinement of both retrieval and generation processes to improve overall reliability
research_gaps: Fine-tuning RAG parameters such as the embedding model or chunk size; Enhancing RAG with structured Building Information Modeling (BIM) data via a function-calling approach with an LLM; Addressing heterogeneous file types in construction projects by using multimodal LLMs

title: A Coal Mine Underground Localization Algorithm Based on the Feature Vector
relevance_reason: The paper uses 'vector' in the signal-processing sense (RSSI signal vectors for fingerprint-based localization) and does not discuss vector databases, vector indexing, or approximate nearest neighbor search as a technology; no vector database system or indexing method is mentioned.
research_focus: Proposing a feature vector-matching algorithm (FVMA) for underground coal mine roadway localization based on RSSI signal fingerprints, aiming to improve positioning accuracy and reduce computation time compared to KNN-based methods.
method: The FVMA algorithm constructs a feature vector database and a distance database from RSSI signals of WiFi APs, divides the sample set into subsets with center vectors, and localizes a received signal by matching its distance to subset centers and comparing signal sources, all evaluated via MATLAB simulation of a 400 m coal mine roadway.
application_domain: Underground coal mine localization and personnel tracking for safety and rescue operations
results_summary: The FVMA algorithm was evaluated in a MATLAB simulation of a 400 m coal mine roadway with 21 WiFi APs and 2000 training points. The maximum localization error was 4 m and the average error was 1.62 m. Within a 1 m error threshold, X-axis accuracy reached 98% while Y-axis accuracy was 86%. The algorithm required significantly less computation time than KNN and WKNN baselines. The authors conclude that FVMA meets the accuracy and real-time requirements of coal mine safety and underground personnel localization systems.
limitations: The Y-axis localization error was slightly larger than the X-axis error, though deemed acceptable due to the limited roadway width; Evaluation was conducted solely through MATLAB simulation rather than a real-world coal mine deployment

title: ChatSOS: Vector database augmented generative question answering assistant in safety engineering
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily a domain application (safety engineering QA) that uses a vector database as a retrieval component within a RAG pipeline; it does not propose, analyze, or benchmark vector database technology itself, and only briefly mentions Milvus and FAISS as examples of existing systems.
research_focus: Development and evaluation of ChatSOS, a vector database-augmented generative question-answering assistant tailored for the safety engineering domain, specifically for answering queries about explosion accidents in China.
method: Construction of a vector database from 117 explosion accident reports using corpus segmenting and vector embedding, combined with a large language model (LLM) for retrieval-augmented generation. The system uses top-k similarity search for retrieval and prompt engineering for task-specific instructions. Evaluation is conducted via a five-dimension weighted scoring framework (Relevance, Accuracy, Comprehensiveness, Adaptability, Clarity) based on expert blind reviews, with comparative experiments against standard LLMs.
mentioned_systems: Milvus; FAISS; ChatGPT; GPTs; Llama; Bard; Gemini; ChatLaw; BiomedRAG; PaperQA
application_domain: Safety engineering, specifically explosion accident analysis and question answering in the Chinese industrial safety context
results_summary: The paper develops ChatSOS by building a vector database from Chinese explosion accident reports (2013-2023) and integrating it with LLMs for retrieval-augmented question answering. Comparative analysis shows that the vector database outperforms a relational database in information retrieval quality, and that ChatSOS significantly enhances reliability, accuracy, and comprehensiveness of LLM responses compared to standard models like ChatGPT. The system also improves adaptability and clarity of responses. The authors demonstrate that prompt engineering with an updatable vector database offers a more convenient and controllable alternative to fine-tuning. However, the top-k retrieval method remains constrained when queries contain multiple keywords.
limitations: The top-k similarity search method is constrained when retrieval terms contain more than one keyword; The system was developed and validated only on a Chinese explosion-accident corpus, limiting cross-domain and multilingual generalization; LLMs used in the system still face inherent limitations due to lack of professional knowledge and model hallucinations
research_gaps: Refining keyword prioritization based on specific query contexts to overcome top-k limitations; Expanding the safety engineering database by incorporating authoritative sources and extracting triplet relationships for knowledge graph construction; Integrating the system into a multi-agent framework with demand analysis, keyword extraction, and graph traversal for improved recall and correlation; Developing specialized domain toolkits for real-time calculations and analyses; Developing intelligent model agents that autonomously plan and coordinate task workflows; Extending applicability to multilingual and cross-domain safety engineering contexts

title: Construction of an Intelligent Risk Identification System for Highway Flood Damage Based on Multimodal Large Models
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about an AI application for highway flood damage identification using MLLMs and RAG; a vectorized indexing mechanism is mentioned only as a component enabling semantic retrieval within the RAG pipeline, with no analysis, comparison, or in-depth discussion of vector database technology.
research_focus: Construction of an intelligent recognition system for highway flood damage identification that integrates a multimodal large language model (Qwen-VL-Max) with a structured domain knowledge base and RAG techniques to improve accuracy and reliability over manual inspection methods.
method: A multi-level structured knowledge base covering eight flood damage categories is built with embedding encoding and semantic tagging. A vectorized indexing mechanism enables semantic retrieval. Task-specific prompt templates and RAG guide the multimodal model to extract risk elements from image-text inputs and generate structured identification results with expert recommendations. The system is evaluated on a real-world highway flood damage dataset.
application_domain: Highway flood damage identification and transportation infrastructure emergency response
results_summary: The paper proposes and evaluates a Road Damage Intelligent Detection System (R-DIDS) that fuses image recognition, a structured flood damage knowledge base, and a multimodal large model in an 'Image-Prompt-Knowledge' tripartite framework. The knowledge-enhanced model outperforms baseline and prompt-optimized models, achieving 91.5% average accuracy, a semantic relevance score of 4.58 out of 5, and 85% robustness under difficult conditions. The system was deployed on the Cherry Studio platform and validated on a real-world highway flood damage dataset. The results demonstrate the practical effectiveness of local deployment and knowledge enhancement for disaster identification in transportation contexts.
research_gaps: Co-optimization of prompt templates and knowledge fragments to improve retrieval efficiency and responsiveness to contextual variation; Exploration of Reasoning-chain control mechanisms such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Tree-of-Thought (ToT) frameworks to enhance multi-step reasoning capabilities; Incorporation of visualized traceability and feedback modules to enhance controllability and engineering adaptability of recognition outputs

title: Classifying and Characterizing Fast Nodular Iron Casting Metallographies by Applying a Similarity Search Method
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily a domain application (metallographic classification in foundries) that uses a vector database and similarity search as a tool; it does not propose, analyze, benchmark, or compare vector database systems or their core indexing technology.
research_focus: Replacing subjective, human-based metallographic classification of nodular iron castings with an objective similarity-search approach that queries a vector database of pre-characterized reference images to determine nodule count and nodularity percentage in real time.
method: Metallography images are embedded using Local Binary Pattern (LBP) followed by PCA dimensionality reduction, stored in a vector database, and queried via Cosine Similarity k-NN search. The final characterization is computed as a similarity-weighted average of the k most similar reference images, following a RAG-like retrieval pattern.
application_domain: Metallographic quality control in iron foundries (nodular iron casting classification)
results_summary: The authors built a vector database of characterized metallography images using LBP+PCA embeddings and performed Cosine Similarity k-NN retrieval to classify new images. They determined that k=2 minimizes error for nodule count and k=21 for nodularity percentage, yielding a maximum deviation of about 8 percentage units in optimal cases. The system is described as pessimistic, avoiding false positives, and deemed feasible for day-to-day foundry use. The approach avoids the computational cost and training complexity of deep learning classifiers while maintaining sufficient accuracy for real-time quality checks.
limitations: The dataset does not cover the full spectrum of possible metallographic values, so unusual or laboratory test images may not yield good characterizations; Classical computer vision methods (LBP) are used for vector representation, which may be less accurate than newer approaches like CNNs; The research was conducted only for one type of iron (nodular iron) and does not cover attacked metallographies or other metal types; Deviations require statistical adjustment factors that have not yet been validated across all classification ranges
research_gaps: Expand the database with unusual metallographies from test and laboratory environments; Implement a minimum similarity threshold to alert users when no sufficiently similar reference image is found; Statistically generate and validate adjustment factors for predicted values across all classification ranges; Explore new image representation mechanisms such as CNNs to improve embedding quality and re-evaluate similarity classification; Extend the method to other types of iron and attacked metallographies; Integrate models for different metal types through orchestration of work pipelines with a type classifier; Incorporate the model into multimodal AI systems with LLMs for improved interaction and querying; Explore transfer learning with pre-trained vision-text models (e.g., Llava) for metallography analysis

title: An Industry Application of Secure Augmentation and Gen-AI for Transforming Engineering Design and Manufacturing
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about an LLM-based RAG application for industrial inventory management; vector databases and ANN search are used as pipeline components but are not the subject of analysis, comparison, or improvement.
research_focus: Integration of LLMs and Gen-AI (specifically RAG with vector search) into industrial inventory management and component selection workflows in a control panel manufacturing facility, with a focus on privacy preservation.
method: A Python-based API pipeline that converts user queries into 384-dimensional vector embeddings using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 transformer model, performs ANN search in a vector database with a 0.7 similarity threshold returning up to five candidates, and then uses an LLM to generate context-aware recommendations. Privacy is maintained through selective obfuscation using the ROT13 algorithm. The vector database dynamically expands as new queries are processed.
application_domain: Industrial manufacturing, specifically inventory management and component selection in a control panel manufacturing facility
results_summary: The paper implemented and tested an LLM-based RAG system for inventory search in a real-world control panel manufacturing environment. The system uses 384-dimensional embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2, ANN search with a 0.7 similarity threshold, and LLM-based recommendation generation. Real-world testing with an industry sponsor demonstrated 88.4% Answer Relevance, 92.1% Faithfulness, 80.2% Context Recall, and 83.1% Context Precision. The vector database dynamically expands with new queries, enabling continuous learning over time. The authors conclude the approach bridges the gap between traditional inventory tools and modern AI capabilities while preserving data privacy.
research_gaps: Extensibility to other domains requiring intelligent inventory or product search is noted as a potential direction

title: AI Enabled Automated Student Q&A Tool: Prof Notes AI
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about an educational AI application for engineering students; Pinecone vector database is only mentioned in passing as one component of the technology stack, with no analysis, benchmarking, or discussion of vector database technology or indexing methods.
research_focus: Whether an AI-driven tool based on professors' notes and course outlines can improve engineering students' learning outcomes by providing immediate, course-specific answers to technical and syllabus-related questions.
method: Development of a full-stack application (React/JavaScript frontend, Python backend) integrating GPT models, Llama, and Pinecone vector databases, deployed on Google App Engine with Firebase for real-time data flow. Evaluation through two rounds of in-person user testing with 18 participants (undergraduate, master's, PhD students, and professors) using a matrix-based framework assessing accuracy, response time, clarity, and usefulness of retrieved resources.
mentioned_systems: Pinecone; GPT models; Llama; ChatGPT; CoPilot; Firebase; Google App Engine
application_domain: Engineering education (mechanical engineering, fluid dynamics course)
results_summary: The paper presents Prof-Notes AI, a full-stack application that categorizes student queries as technical or syllabus-related and retrieves relevant content from professor notes, including equations, illustrations, and videos. User testing with 18 participants across two rounds showed that linking answers directly to professor notes improved response relevance, and many students found the tool reliable. However, some users noted challenges with complex, multi-step queries and the system's inability to analyze trends in visual data. Students appreciated the seamless cross-device experience, though adoption remained limited due to low awareness. The authors conclude that the tool effectively preserves instructor-specific pedagogy but requires improvements in answer depth, response ranking, and interactive discussion capabilities.
limitations: The system cannot yet analyze or interpret complex trends from supporting visual data (e.g., graphs); Responses to complex, multi-step questions need improvement; Limited student adoption due to lack of awareness about the platform's syllabus alignment and structured learning approach; Reliance on other resources noted by some users
research_gaps: Integrating trend analysis and automated graphical interpretations as part of response generation; Enhancing interactive discussions with the AI for active learning; Improving response ranking for better accuracy; Conducting quantitative, comparative studies between Prof-Notes AI and general-purpose AI tools like ChatGPT and CoPilot; Optimizing system performance to reduce response time; Developing a targeted marketing strategy to raise awareness and integrate the tool into students' routines
